title: India Just Made Government Bonds Tax-Free for Foreign Investors. Here Is What NRIs Need to Know.
excerpt: New Delhi has scrapped capital gains tax and the 20 per cent withholding tax on interest from government securities for foreign investors, effective retroactively from April 2026. The move is designed to stop the rupee's slide — but it also reshapes the math for every NRI weighing Indian debt exposure.
body:
On June 5, the Indian government promulgated the Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 — a technical-sounding document that carries a very non-technical message: if you are a foreign investor holding Indian government bonds, your profits are now tax-free.

The ordinance inserts new entries 13D and 13E into Schedule IV of the Income-tax Act, exempting foreign institutional investors and the Bank for International Settlements from tax on both interest income and capital gains arising from government securities. The exemption applies retroactively from April 1, 2026.

For the roughly four million NRIs in the United States alone, this is not just a policy signal — it is a material change in the risk-return calculation for Indian fixed income.

## What Actually Changed

Before the ordinance, foreign portfolio investors paid a 12.5 per cent long-term capital gains tax on listed government bonds held for more than 12 months. They also faced a 20 per cent withholding tax on interest earned from those bonds.

Both are now gone.

The government has simultaneously expanded the Fully Accessible Route — the channel through which foreign investors can buy Indian government bonds without quantitative limits. New issuances in 15-year, 30-year, and 40-year tenors are now included, along with Sovereign Green Bonds. Three existing restrictions on foreign portfolio investment — the short-term investment limit, concentration limit, and security-wise limit — have been removed.

The RBI accompanied this with its own measures: concessional forex swaps until September 30 to encourage state-owned firms to tap dollar borrowings, and hedging cost compensation for banks on three-year and five-year FCNR deposits aimed at the Indian diaspora.

## Why New Delhi Did This Now

The timing is not subtle. The rupee has fallen over 5 per cent in 2026, touching a record low near 95.96 against the dollar. Foreign investors have pulled roughly $27.6 billion out of Indian equities since January — the largest sustained exit in years. Brent crude surged past $96 a barrel after Iran fired missiles at Israel, widening India's trade deficit.

India's foreign exchange reserves have dropped from $728 billion to $682 billion in three months — a $46 billion decline that signals the RBI has been spending heavily to defend the rupee with limited success.

The government needed dollar inflows. Fast. And with equities bleeding capital, the bond market was the logical place to build a new wall.

Larsen & Toubro's group chief economist Sachchidanand Shukla estimates the combined measures could draw $40 to $60 billion in fresh inflows. Whether that materialises depends on how foreign investors weigh the tax relief against the underlying risks — rising inflation, a potential rate hike, and continued geopolitical volatility.

## What This Means for NRIs

NRIs are not the direct target of this ordinance. The exemption applies to Foreign Portfolio Investors — registered institutional entities — and the Bank for International Settlements. Individual NRIs investing through NRE or NRO accounts are governed by different tax rules.

But the indirect effects matter.

First, the policy signals that India is willing to use aggressive tax policy to stabilise the rupee and attract foreign capital into its debt market. For NRIs holding rupee-denominated assets — property, fixed deposits, mutual funds — a stabilised rupee protects the dollar value of those holdings.

Second, the expansion of the Fully Accessible Route and the removal of investment caps on government bonds could increase foreign demand for Indian sovereign debt, pushing bond prices up and yields down. NRIs who already hold Indian government bond funds or gilt mutual funds could benefit from capital appreciation.

Third, and most practically: the RBI's hedging cost compensation on FCNR deposits is directly relevant. Indian banks are racing to offer NRIs 5 per cent or higher returns on dollar-denominated deposits with the government effectively subsidising the hedging cost. If you have surplus dollars sitting in a US savings account earning 4 per cent after tax, the FCNR window — open until September 30 — may offer a better risk-adjusted return with sovereign backing.

## The Risks Are Real

This is not a risk-free trade, and the government's urgency is itself a signal.

The rupee has been depreciating because the fundamentals have deteriorated. India's current account deficit is widening. Oil prices remain elevated. The RBI held rates steady last week but signalled a potential hike is coming — which would increase borrowing costs for the government and could push bond prices down.

The tax exemption was introduced via ordinance rather than parliamentary legislation, giving it immediate legal force but raising questions about permanence. Political polling cited by *Reuters* suggests the move is seen by some as giving undue benefits to foreign investors, which makes it potentially fragile in an election-sensitive environment.

And while the FCNR deposit window is genuinely attractive, NRIs should understand what they are buying: a three-to-five-year lock-in denominated in dollars but carrying Indian counterparty risk. If the rupee depreciates further, the bank's hedging costs rise, and the RBI's commitment to subsidise those costs expires in September.

## The Bottom Line

India has never offered foreign investors tax-free access to its sovereign debt market. The fact that it is doing so now — retroactively, by ordinance, alongside a suite of emergency rupee-support measures — tells you everything about how seriously New Delhi views the current macro situation.

For NRIs, the practical takeaway is narrow but real: if you were considering FCNR deposits, the window is open and the terms are the best they have been in years. If you hold Indian government bond funds, the foreign demand wave could lift your returns. And if you have been watching the rupee slide from the sidelines, this is the clearest signal yet that the government will spend political and fiscal capital to stabilise it.

Whether that is enough depends on oil, the Fed, and the next RBI meeting. But the tax-free door is open — and it will not stay open forever.

Sources: Reuters, Outlook Money, CAClubIndia, NRI Globe, Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance 2026
